name: Plebański-Hacyan Spacetimes and Anti-Nariai
description: The products of two surfaces of constant curvature that solve the Einstein-Maxwell equations with a cosmological constant beside Nariai's and Bertotti and Robinson's: a flat plane of time and space times a sphere, anti-de Sitter space of two dimensions times a flat plane, and the anti-Nariai universe, anti-de Sitter space of two dimensions times a hyperbolic plane. The first two hold a uniform electromagnetic field whose energy density matches the cosmological constant, and anti-Nariai is a vacuum.
convention: We keep factors of $c$ and $G$ explicit. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: Multiply two surfaces together, each curved the same at every point, a flat sheet, a sphere, or a saddle that runs on forever, and let one of them carry the time: which of these products does Einstein's gravity accept? With an electromagnetic field and a cosmological constant $\Lambda$ allowed, two numbers decide, the curvature $K_1$ of the surface that carries the time and the curvature $K_2$ of the other [ortaggio2002direct]. The cosmological constant is their average, $\Lambda = (K_1 + K_2)/2$, and the energy density $\varepsilon$ of the field is set by their difference, $8\pi G\varepsilon/c^4 = (K_2 - K_1)/2$ [ortaggio2002direct]. A field has no negative energy, so $K_2$ cannot be the smaller, and of the nine ways to choose flat, positive, or negative twice, Marcello Ortaggio and Jiří Podolský struck out three in 2002 [ortaggio2002direct].¶Two flat sheets make Minkowski space, and two surfaces of the same positive curvature make the universe of Hidekazu Nariai, a vacuum with positive $\Lambda$ whose Euclidean form, a pair of equal spheres, Edward Kasner had published in 1925 [ortaggio2002direct, nariai1950, kasner1925]. Anti-de Sitter space of two dimensions times a sphere holds a uniform electromagnetic field, and is the universe of Bruno Bertotti and Ivor Robinson, who each found it in 1959 [bertotti1959, robinson1959]. Bertotti kept the cosmological constant, and described his manifold as the product of "two ordinary surfaces of constant curvature, whose type and radius depend on the values of the cosmological constant and the invariants of the electromagnetic field" [bertotti1959].¶Jerzy Plebański and Shahen Hacyan, working in Mexico City, came to two of the other products in 1979 from a different direction: the solutions of the Einstein-Maxwell equations with a cosmological constant that are of type D, with two special families of light rays, both lined up with the field [plebanski1979exceptional]. Usually the equations then make those rays travel as free light does, along geodesics and without shear, but that conclusion fails when the energy density of the field equals $|\Lambda|c^4/8\pi G$ [ortaggio2002direct]. Plebański and Hacyan worked out those exceptions [plebanski1979exceptional, ortaggio2002direct]. Two of the three are products with one flat factor: a flat plane of time and space times a sphere when $\Lambda > 0$, and anti-de Sitter space of two dimensions times a flat plane when $\Lambda < 0$ [ortaggio2002direct]. The third has $\Lambda < 0$, is not a product, carries an arbitrary function of a retarded time, and, in their words, "admits no Killing vectors" [ortaggio2002direct, plebanski1979exceptional].¶In the first, the positive cosmological constant pushes and the field pulls, and the curvature of the plane of time and $z$ is the one less the other, $K_1 = \Lambda - 8\pi G\varepsilon/c^4$, which vanishes [ortaggio2002direct]. So that plane is as flat as special relativity's, and every sphere has the area $2\pi/\Lambda$ [ortaggio2002direct]. How does the second come by a flat plane of space? There a negative $\Lambda$ undoes the field in the other surface, $K_2 = \Lambda + 8\pi G\varepsilon/c^4 = 0$, and time and one direction of space form an anti-de Sitter space of two dimensions, as they do in Bertotti and Robinson's universe [ortaggio2002direct, bertotti1959]. Each has six symmetries: those of its two dimensional spacetime, together with the rotations of the sphere in the first and with the shifts and turns of the plane in the second [ortaggio2002direct].¶With both curvatures negative and equal there is no field, and anti-de Sitter space of two dimensions times a hyperbolic plane is a vacuum with $\Lambda < 0$, which Ortaggio called "anti-Nariai" in 2002 [ortaggio2002]. The limit that turns a black hole into such a product goes back to 1983, when Paul Ginsparg and Malcolm Perry let the two horizons of a black hole in de Sitter space close on each other and were left with Nariai's universe [ginsparg1983]. Twenty one years later Vitor Cardoso, Óscar Dias, and José Lemos took the same limit for the static charged black holes of de Sitter and anti-de Sitter space [cardoso2004]. The flat plane times a sphere came out where the three horizons of a charged hole in de Sitter space meet, anti-de Sitter space times a plane from the charged holes of anti-de Sitter space with flat horizons, and anti-Nariai from those with hyperbolic horizons, the one case that needs no charge [cardoso2004]. The hole whose horizon is a closed surface of negative curvature had already given Marco Caldarelli, Luciano Vanzo, and Sergio Zerbini that last product in 2000 [caldarelli2001extremal].¶Anti-Nariai is homogeneous and has the causal structure of anti-de Sitter space of two dimensions, but far away it does not approach anti-de Sitter space of four dimensions, since its hyperbolic plane keeps one size [dias2003]. Can a gravitational wave cross universes this uniform? For Plebański and Hacyan's two products Ortaggio and Podolský built such waves in 2002, impulses made by particles travelling at the speed of light with any multipole structure, which at $\Lambda = 0$ become the pp-waves of flat space [ortaggio2002direct]. A year on, the two of them wrote all of these universes, the one without symmetry included, as members of Wolfgang Kundt's class, whose light rays neither spread nor twist, with gravitational waves of any profile running through them [podolsky2003kundt].

related.text: The product with both curvatures positive and equal, de Sitter space of two dimensions times a sphere, a vacuum with $\Lambda > 0$ [nariai1950, ortaggio2002direct]. Anti-Nariai is its counterpart with $\Lambda < 0$ and takes its name from it [ortaggio2002].

Anti-de Sitter space of two dimensions times a sphere, the uniform electromagnetic field with no cosmological constant. Bruno Bertotti's solution of 1959 allowed one, with two surfaces whose type and radius depend on it and on the field [bertotti1959].
The black holes of anti-de Sitter space with hyperbolic horizons. At the least mass that keeps a horizon, the limit toward that horizon is anti-Nariai [caldarelli2001extremal, cardoso2004].
The charged black hole in de Sitter space. In the limit where its three horizons meet, the region between them is the flat plane times a sphere [cardoso2004].
Time and one direction of space form an anti-de Sitter space of two dimensions, of radius $a$, in the product with a flat plane and in anti-Nariai [ortaggio2002direct].

A pair of accelerating black holes. Óscar Dias and José Lemos took the limit toward a degenerate horizon of the C-metric with $\Lambda < 0$ and found the anti-Nariai C-metric, which is anti-Nariai when the acceleration vanishes [dias2003].

coordinates.name: Sphere

parameters.description: Radius of every sphere, a length; it fixes the cosmological constant, $\Lambda = 1/2b^2$, and the energy density $\varepsilon$ of the uniform electromagnetic field, $8\pi G\varepsilon/c^4 = \Lambda$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, z, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ a time and $z$ a length along the flat factor. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Sphere, Rindler

parameters.description: Radius of every sphere, a length; it fixes the cosmological constant, $\Lambda = 1/2b^2$, and the energy density $\varepsilon$ of the uniform electromagnetic field, $8\pi G\varepsilon/c^4 = \Lambda$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(\tau, \chi, \theta, \phi)$, with $\tau$ a boost angle and $\chi$ a length, related to the inertial chart by $ct = \chi\sinh\tau$ and $z = \chi\cosh\tau$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

coordinates.name: Plane

parameters.description: Radius of the anti-de Sitter factor, a length; it fixes the cosmological constant, $\Lambda = -1/2a^2$, and the energy density $\varepsilon$ of the uniform electromagnetic field, $8\pi G\varepsilon/c^4 = -\Lambda$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(u, w, x, y)$, all lengths, with $u$ a retarded time, $w$ along the rays of constant $u$, and $x$ and $y$ Cartesian on the flat plane. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

coordinates.name: Plane, Null

parameters.description: Radius of the anti-de Sitter factor, a length; it fixes the cosmological constant, $\Lambda = -1/2a^2$, and the energy density $\varepsilon$ of the uniform electromagnetic field, $8\pi G\varepsilon/c^4 = -\Lambda$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(u, v, x, y)$, all lengths, with $u$ and $v$ null and $x$ and $y$ Cartesian on the flat plane; Plebański and Hacyan's $w$ is $v/(1 + uv/2a^2)$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

coordinates.name: Plane, Static

parameters.description: Radius of the anti-de Sitter factor, a length; it fixes the cosmological constant, $\Lambda = -1/2a^2$, and the energy density $\varepsilon$ of the uniform electromagnetic field, $8\pi G\varepsilon/c^4 = -\Lambda$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(\tau, \chi, x, y)$, with $\tau$ and $\chi$ dimensionless on the anti-de Sitter factor and $x$ and $y$ Cartesian lengths on the flat plane. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

coordinates.name: Anti-Nariai

parameters.description: Common radius of the anti-de Sitter factor and the hyperbolic plane, a length; it fixes the cosmological constant, $\Lambda = -1/a^2$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(\tau, \chi, \theta, \phi)$, all dimensionless, with $\tau$ and $\chi$ on the anti-de Sitter factor and $\theta$ and $\phi$ polar on the hyperbolic plane. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

coordinates.name: Anti-Nariai, Static

parameters.description: Common radius of the anti-de Sitter factor and the hyperbolic plane, a length; it fixes the cosmological constant, $\Lambda = -1/a^2$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ a time, $r = a\cosh\chi$ a length, and $\theta$ and $\phi$ polar on the hyperbolic plane. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Exceptional

parameters.description: Radius of the anti-de Sitter factor, a length; it fixes the cosmological constant, $\Lambda = -1/2a^2$, and the energy density $\varepsilon$ of the uniform electromagnetic field, $8\pi G\varepsilon/c^4 = -\Lambda$

Any function of $u$, an inverse length; with $g$ it tilts the light cones across the flat plane, and with $f = g = 0$ the spacetime is the product of anti-de Sitter space of two dimensions and the plane
Any function of $u$, an inverse length, the counterpart of $f$ along $y$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(u, w, x, y)$, all lengths, with $u$ a retarded time and $x$ and $y$ Cartesian. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.
